# Independent audit: occupied-parity centers with strict minimal-face mass


occupied-parity-weighted-center-strict-face-theorem-simplex-chains.md.

**Result: PASS.** This audit concerns the stated finite weighted
base theorem and its midpoint-label extension. It does not infer a
mixed-integer halfspace-depth theorem for nonaffine fiber-centroid
graphs.

## 1. Exact theorem and exceptional configuration

For a finite complete intersection \(P=\operatorname{conv}(P)\cap\Lambda\)
in an affine lattice, positive weights of total \(M\), and \(k\)
occupied parity classes, the source proves that a point of \(P\)
has weighted depth at least \(\alpha=M/k\). Moreover some such
point has minimal-face weight strictly greater than \(\alpha\),
unless \(P\) consists of \(k\) equally weighted vertices.

The exception is exact. In it, each point's own positive atom
gives depth at least \(\alpha\), while the halfspace exposing
that vertex gives depth at most \(\alpha\). Its minimal face is
the singleton of that same weight.

The rank-zero case and \(k=1\) case are included. A finite
one-parity complete set with two distinct points would contain
their midpoint, contradicting the shortest distance between
two distinct points. Thus it is a singleton and is precisely
the exceptional case. No estimate involving ambient dimension
is needed.

## 2. Occupied-parity Helly argument

I checked each strictness transition in Lemma 1.

* Empty feasibility of the original closed inequalities gives a
  strictly positive minimum violation over the finite nonempty \(P\).
  Increasing each original threshold by a common smaller positive
  amount still leaves the corresponding strict system infeasible.
* The threshold set is a closed subset of the stated finite box:
  its coverage condition is a finite intersection of finite unions
  of closed inequalities. It is nonempty and compact, so the sum
  of thresholds attains its maximum.
* At a nonsaturated coordinate, failure to have a private boundary
  witness would permit a strictly positive increase of that
  coordinate. Finiteness supplies the minimum positive gap among
  private points; when there are no private points, any sufficiently
  small increase works. Both cases contradict maximality.
* Two private boundary witnesses in one parity class have an
  actual midpoint in \(P\). At their two distinguished constraints
  one endpoint has equality and the other strict inequality.
  At every other constraint both are strict. The midpoint therefore
  satisfies the entire strict system, a contradiction.
* Saturated constraints are strictly satisfied by every point of
  \(P\), because their upper box thresholds exceed all evaluations.
  The at most \(k\) nonsaturated constraints alone exclude \(P\).
  Their original closed constraints are stronger than these strict
  constraints, due to the initial positive threshold increase.

This proves the claimed finite inequality Helly statement without
using a lattice-dimension bound, a maximal lattice-free polyhedron,
or an unproved characterization of finite-set Helly numbers.
Paired halfspaces for affine-hull equations correctly handle
lower-dimensional polytopes in Lemma 2.

## 3. An independent direct proof of the needed center guarantee

The following alternative argument was derived before reading the
source. It independently verifies the parity mechanism and its
boundary conventions.

First, any finite closed-halfspace cover of \(P\) has a subcover
of at most \(k\) original halfspaces. Select an inclusion-minimal
subcover
\[
 H_i=\{a_i(z)\ge b_i\},\quad i=1,\ldots,m.
\]
Each \(H_i\) has an original private point \(r_i\): it lies in
\(H_i\) and lies strictly outside every other cap. Increase the
thresholds while preserving coverage, and maximize their sum.
The feasible set is nonempty, closed, and bounded, since
\[
 b_i\le c_i\le a_i(r_i)
\]
for every feasible threshold vector: increasing other thresholds
cannot make any other cap cover \(r_i\).

At a maximizing vector every cap has a private point exactly
on its boundary. If all its private points had positive margin,
finiteness would allow another small threshold increase. Two
private boundary points in the same parity class would have an
integral midpoint in \(P\) strictly outside every tightened cap.
Thus \(m\le k\). Since tightening only shrank the caps, this also
proves the assertion for the original caps.

If no \(\alpha=M/k\) center existed, choose for each point a
closed halfspace containing it of weight strictly below
\(\alpha\). These caps cover \(P\), hence have an at most
\(k\)-member subcover. Their weights sum to strictly less than
\(k\alpha=M\), contradicting coverage of all positive weights.
This proves the center guarantee independently.

Both proofs retain points on closed boundaries. The private
boundary contact is included in its own cap; its midpoint with
another private contact lies strictly outside every cap.

## 4. Fractional tight-face partition

The source's finite strict separation step is valid. For
the tight-face incidence vectors \(\chi_F\), if
\((1/k)\mathbf1\) is outside their convex hull, strict
separation gives a vector \(v\) satisfying
\[
 v\cdot\chi_F<\frac1k\sum_pv_p.
\]
Writing \(w\) for the positive weight vector and
\[
 v'=v-\frac{\sum_pv_p}{M}\,w
\]
gives both \(\sum_pv'_p=0\) and \(v'\cdot\chi_F<0\),
because \(w(F)=M/k\) for every tight face.
Thus failure of such a signed perturbation yields
\[
 \sum_F\lambda_F\chi_F=\mathbf1,\qquad
 \lambda_F\ge0,\qquad \sum_F\lambda_F=k.                 \tag{A}
\]
The coefficient total is exact, not bounded up to a constant.

For two same-parity points \(p,q\), their midpoint \(m\)
belongs to \(P\). For every actual face,
\[
 \chi_F(m)=\chi_F(p)\chi_F(q).
\]
Therefore each summand
\(\chi_F(p)+\chi_F(q)-2\chi_F(m)\) is nonnegative.
Its weighted sum under (A) is zero, so all three incidences
agree for every positive-coefficient face.

There are at most \(k\) incidence patterns. Every pattern
class is contained in a positive-coefficient tight face,
since its weighted incidence sum is 1. Consequently every
class has weight at most \(\alpha\). Their total weight
\(k\alpha\) forces exactly \(k\) classes, each of weight
\(\alpha\).

At this point, and not earlier, the map from the \(k\)
occupied parities to the \(k\) classes is a bijection.
Each class now has one parity and is midpoint-closed.
The shortest-pair argument makes each class a singleton.
Every selected tight face then has exactly one point;
because it is a face of \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\), it is
a vertex. Coverage by (A) makes every point a vertex.
This proves precisely the claimed exceptional configuration.
Conversely its singleton tight faces exclude a zero-sum
strictly negative perturbation.

No midpoint-component closure assumption appears in this
argument. Incidence classes are forced to be single-parity
only after the exact class-count equality is proved.

## 5. Fixed perturbation and the selected original center

The source chooses one small positive \(\epsilon\), not a
limit. The perturbed weights \(w+\epsilon v\) retain their
total \(M\) and therefore retain the same threshold
\(\alpha\). Their positivity is preserved by finiteness.

Every halfspace trace is a subset of \(P\), so the number
of traces is finite. The source's bound
\[
 |\delta_w(p)-\delta_{w'}(p)|
 \le\sum_q|w_q-w'_q|
\]
is valid for the minimum of these finitely many sums.
The strictly positive gaps at old noncenters therefore
ensure that every perturbed center is an original center.
Finitely many old subcritical face masses remain
subcritical; all tight face masses strictly decrease by
the chosen perturbation.

An exposing halfspace for the minimal face of a perturbed
center gives perturbed minimal-face mass at least
\(\alpha\). Its old minimal-face mass thus cannot be at
most \(\alpha\). This proves the strict inequality for
a single point of the original \(P\). A fixed ordering
selects one deterministically if desired.

All proper faces of the polytope are exposed, including
when its affine hull is smaller than the ambient affine
space. For \(k\ge2\) the full face has mass \(M>\alpha\);
it causes no exception in the face perturbation.

## 6. Midpoint-label extension

The Section 7 extension is valid with exactly its stated
hypothesis: every pair with the same occupied label has
its actual geometric midpoint in \(P\). No label is
prescribed for that midpoint initially.

The Helly proof only needs the existence of that point.
The incidence proof then gives identical endpoint and
midpoint patterns. Only after the number of patterns
equals the number of labels does the bijection force
the midpoint to share its endpoints' label. The same
finite midpoint-closure argument applies.

For a lifted graph this requires
\[
 g_{(p+q)/2}=(g_p+g_q)/2
\]
for every same-parity pair, as the source explicitly
states. Equality on a selected subset of pairs would
not establish the extension. No such equality for
general fiber centroids is inferred by either source
or audit.

The audit uses finite exact arguments throughout.
No numerical verification or unproved OC consequence
is needed.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
